title: Chicago entrepreneur turns empty downtown office space into vertical gardens
description:
The pandemic changed how and where the world works, leaving behind a lot of empty office space. One entrepreneur is starting to plant the seeds of a partial solution.

MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST: Years after pandemic restrictions subsided, many downtown business districts still are not as busy as they were. So what to do with all those empty offices? Well, in Chicago, an entrepreneur has some creative ideas. Here's reporter Al Orendorff.AL ORENDORFF, BYLINE: I'm standing outside one of downtown Chicago's office towers. Ever since the post-COVID world made a return to the office possible, cities like Chicago have recovered some of their empty office space, but not all.RUSSELL STEINBERG: There's a line of sight on solving some really complicated problems, three of them specifically - office vacancy, public health crisis and food system challenges.ORENDORFF: That's Russell Steinberg, founder and CEO of FARMZER0. His company uses empty downtown office space to grow edible greens that he then delivers to restaurants, caterers, other office buildings and folks who live in nearby high-rises. The only prerequisite is vacant space. He says there's about 45 million square feet of that in Chicago.STEINBERG: The amount of square footage that we would need to convert to feed everyone in the entire city of Chicago the adequate vegetables is, like, 2 million square feet out of the 45 million.ORENDORFF: Chicago's downtown business district's post-pandemic recovery has left it with a roughly 25- to 30% vacancy rate. Steinberg says much of the vacant space is in the older office buildings. Older infrastructures make them harder to repurpose. The newer commercial space makes up some of the vacancies as well, but because they're newer, they're more easily reused. At this FARMZER0 location, the plan for repurposing commercial space uses about 650 square feet of vacant office area.(SOUNDBITE OF WATER RUNNING)ORENDORFF: And while there's always water running to keep the plants hydrated, it's not as much water as you might think. Steinberg says less than what might be used in a fully functioning office. It's a remarkably quiet operation, except when somebody brings out the scissors to do a little harvesting.(SOUNDBITE OF SCISSORS CUTTING)ORENDORFF: What FARMZER0 produces is an important part of what Blue Plate Chicago's catering service sells. Chef Matthew Wilde sees his business association with vertical farming as a win-win.MATTHEW WILDE: They're utilizing space in downtown Chicago that would otherwise be vacant, and, you know, they're growing a really clean farm-to-table green in an urban setting, which is really cool. And then, in the end, you know, it's a high-quality product, and, you know, supporting local farms, even if it's in an urban setting, is all something that's really important to Blue Plate.ORENDORFF: Northwestern University's civil and environmental engineering professor, Dr. Kimberly Gray, has done a lot of research on how cities can and should reinvent themselves. She considers vertical farming a viable, more climate-friendly option as metro areas around the country rethink their future.KIMBERLY GRAY: I think what it can do is it can bring fresh produce to urban communities in a way that's probably cheaper. It can reduce this notion of the last mile. So the delivery of goods and services in urban settings can be highly polluting.ORENDORFF: FARMZER0's Steinberg says he's had inquiries from a number of cities about replicating the high-rise farming idea. He hopes to partner with city officials in Los Angeles to cook up something special for the 2028 Olympics.For NPR News, I'm Al Orendorff in Chicago.(SOUNDBITE OF SAM TOMPKINS SONG, "SEE ME") Copyright © 2026 NPR.
